headline: Monhegan pollock on top, mackerel holding the bay together
subhead: Groundfish still down in the channels, bass working the river mouths at first light, and the mackerel schools are doing more work than they get credit for.
body_markdown:
Back in the late 80s I had a sternman, Dale, who used to say the bay didn't care what the calendar said — it fished the way it fished, and your job was to figure out which day you'd gotten. Forty years later that's still the only forecasting system I trust. This week the bay gave us a pretty fair hand, provided you were willing to run early and fish the tide instead of the clock.

Starting with what's easy: mackerel are thick from Ram Island out past The Cuckolds, and they've been thick for two weeks now, which is exactly what's kept the striper program alive in the tidal rivers. You don't hear much fuss made over mackerel, but they're the reason there's bait to hold bass in the Sheepscot and up around Wiscasset on the last of the ebb. I had a customer Tuesday morning jigging a small chrome Diamond jig off the Sheepscot bridge pilings at first light, and inside forty minutes he'd boated eight mackerel and had two decent stripers — one a hair under 30 inches — follow a school right up into the current seam and swat at his jig on the retrieve. Switched him to a 6-inch olive Slug-Go, weightless, and let it swing dead-drift through that seam, and that's when the bass started eating for real. Nothing huge, mostly 24 to 28 inches, but a solid dozen fish over two hours on the dropping tide before the sun got up over the trees and shut it down.

That's the pattern right now, and it's the same one we called last week — conditions here have stayed stable, water's held in that comfortable mid-to-high 50s range close to shore, cooler out in the bay proper, and that's kept our stripers shallower and more willing to feed in daylight than what you're seeing from the Cape Cod Canal on south, where the heat's pushed everything down to a dawn-dusk program. We're the lucky zone this time of year. I don't say that often.

Offshore and down around Monhegan, the story's been groundfish, and it's been a genuinely good week for it. Pollock are up on the surface around the ledges off the eastern side of the island — Norton Ledge and out toward Smutty Nose — chasing pogies and sand eels in that nervous, boiling way pollock do when they're really into bait. I had a report from a captain I trust who ran out there Saturday on the last two hours of the incoming and found pollock busting the surface for a good twenty minutes straight, took fish to 8 pounds on white bucktails and swimming plugs cast right into the melee. That's a fun fish to catch on top, and it doesn't last — usually blows out once the tide turns and the bait scatters, so you've got a window, not an all-day bite.

Down deeper, in that 90 to 130 foot water off Monhegan's western side and out toward the deeper channels between the island and Matinicus, cod are still holding where they always hold this time of year — hard bottom, ledge edges, structure that breaks up the current. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, working them slow off bottom, has been the most consistent producer. Sizes have been modest — most fish 3 to 6 pounds, a few pushing 10 — but for late July that's about what you'd expect and about what we've been getting for years now out there. Haddock have been scarcer, a few mixed in on the same drifts but nothing to build a trip around specifically.

Eastern Egg Rock continues to hold its bass in that scrappy, opportunistic way it does all summer — stripers working the edges where the current runs past the rock, feeding on whatever the tide pushes past, sand eels mostly. Light tackle, small soft plastics, nothing fancy. Not a numbers fishery but a reliable one if you're passing by on the way out to Monhegan and want to make a stop.

Penobscot Bay itself has been quieter than I'd like to report. The deeper channels off Vinalhaven and down toward Isle au Haut still hold some groundfish — pollock mostly, a scattering of cod on the drop-offs — but it's spotty work, and I heard from two different boats this week that put in three, four hours and had to work hard for a handful of keepers. If you're going to fish the bay proper right now, fish the tide change hard, right at the top or bottom, and don't waste time on slack water. That's when what fish are there tend to feed.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. Water temps in close have stayed steady, mackerel show no sign of thinning out, and as long as that bait stays put the striper bite in the rivers and around the bay mouths should keep holding through the week. Monhegan's groundfish should stay put too — that's deep, cool water and it doesn't turn on a dime. If I had one day to fish this week I'd run out to Monhegan on a rising tide, hit the ledges for pollock on top first light, then work down to cod once the surface bite dies, and finish the day back in close chasing bass off the river mouths on the evening ebb. Long day, but that's about as complete a Midcoast trip as you're going to string together right now.
